abstract: |
  Calibration is an important property of probabilistic models. It measures the match between predicted probability in a given range and the observed frequency. We study the behavior of linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and commonly used variants of the logistic model in the case of large group separation. When the groups follow homoscedastic normal distribution, the Bayes classifier is well approximated by LDA. All models generally agree on the boundary between classes. However, logistic regression variants consistently overestimate the true probability---a behavior we call multiplicative miscalibration. Currently used miscalibration detection techniques are not well suited to uncover this phenomenon. The odds between true probabilities and predicted probabilities may differ by several orders of magnitude even for commonly encountered effect sizes. We outline several practical applications in finance and multiclass classification, where multiplicative miscalibration could pose severe problems.
---

# Introduction

Probabilistic modelling provides answer to the quintessential question of probability theory: "What is the probability of an event". In classroom setting, the answer is typically a single number which is deduced from modelling assumptions. For instance, we may assume that we roll a perfectly symmetrical dice or, that subsequent throws are independent. In practical applications, however, the question to quantify probability is often asked *repeatedly* with varying context. One naturally expects that the answer will vary depending on the context. For instance, a bank may wonder what is the probability that the borrower will repay a loan. The context could be provided by the current financial disclosure of the applicant. To answer the question it is customary to build a *probabilistic model*. <!-- which is really an algorithm taking input (the context) and producing the desired probability as its output. -->

There is a multitude of ways to build different models, and thus one may ask how to compare their quality. Non-probabilistic ways of comparison use the $2\times 2$ contingency matrix with rows and columns corresponding to predictions (probability \> 0.5) and observed outcomes. One can use any number of metrics for comparison starting from accuracy (ratio of the sum diagonal entries to that of the whole matrix), through precision and recall to Matthews correlation coefficient [@yule1912methods; @chicco2021matthews]. However, this approach disregards much of the probabilistic information.

Historically, the question of how to measure the quality of probabilistic predictions arose in the context of weather forecasting [@glenn1950verification]. First probabilistic forecasts appeared in the early 20th century [@hallenbeck1920forecasting] and became routine since the 1960's [@murphy1984probability]. A simple check of how good weather forecasters (or more precisely their models) are, is to compare their predictions with climate observations. *Climate* is obtained by computing the expected event frequency over long-term (one or more years). If the probability of rain on any given day in a year is 40%, we can compare that with the average probability that was provided by the forecaster throughout the whole year. For a good forecaster, they should be close.

There is an even finer method to compare forecast's fidelity. We can subdivide the probability interval $[0,1]$ into (nonintersecting) subintervals. For each subinterval, we compare the observed frequency of rain on days when the forecast fell into it [@zadrozny2001obtaining]. Suppose for instance that one of the subintervals was $I_m = [0.45, 0.55]$. We would expect that the probability $p$ of rain on days when forecast fell into $I_m$ would be around 0.5 A model that matches this expectation reasonably well is said to be *well-calibrated*. Calibration is typically judged visually by preparing a reliability diagram. or by computing a score such as expected calibration error.

In our paper we will discuss *multiplicative miscalibration* in the context of logistic models. This phenomenon is not detected by currently used techniques, yet may have significant repercussions in applications.

# Logistic models

A model can be viewed as an algorithm, whose input is the context, and the output is the desired probability. The usual mathematical representation of context is a vector. It maybe called vector of features, if features were handpicked, or the embedding vector, if the vector is produced by a neural network. By a *logistic model* we mean an algorithm that for a given context vector $\mathbf{x}$ outputs the probability of a context-dependent event by the following formula $$
P(event \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}),\quad\textrm{where } \sigma(x) = \frac{\exp x}{1 + \exp{x}}.
$$ {#eq-logistic} Note that the model allows predicting probabilities in the whole range $(0,1)$ since $$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty} \sigma(x) = 0, \quad \textrm{and}\quad
\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty} \sigma(x) = 1.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-logistic2}

The two principal examples of logistic models are linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and logistic regression [@james2021introduction]. They both yield prediction in the form @eq-logistic, but they differ in their parameters, as well as in the methods to estimate them. Although logistic regression is more commonly used, they are considered to give approximately the same results. We can illustrate it on the famous iris dataset. The iris dataset was created in 1930's by Edgar Anderson, an American botanist. It contains four measurements (features) of three iris species

-   *Iris versicolor L.* (L. indicates it was named by famous Swedish biologist Carl Linnaeus),
-   *Iris virginica L.*,
-   *Iris setosa*.

From statistical point of view the important property of the dataset is that the features are approximately normally distributed. We can check this for one of the measurements (the width of petal) with normal quantile-quantile plots, shown in @fig-qq: for both versicolor and virginica the points fall close to the reference line, indicating approximate normality.

<!-- Having established this, we compare the class-conditional distributions of the same measurement in @fig-density. -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-qq
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Normal Q-Q plots of Petal.Width for versicolor and virginica. Points close to the reference line indicate that the class-conditional distribution is approximately normal.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.2
d_qq <- droplevels(subset(iris, Species %in% c("versicolor", "virginica")))

col_versicolor <- "#1b9e77"
col_virginica  <- "#d95f02"

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))

pw_versicolor <- d_qq$Petal.Width[d_qq$Species == "versicolor"]
qqnorm(pw_versicolor, col = col_versicolor, pch = 19,
       main = "versicolor", xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
       ylab = "Petal.Width")
qqline(pw_versicolor, col = col_versicolor, lwd = 2)

pw_virginica <- d_qq$Petal.Width[d_qq$Species == "virginica"]
qqnorm(pw_virginica, col = col_virginica, pch = 19,
       main = "virginica", xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
       ylab = "Petal.Width")
qqline(pw_virginica, col = col_virginica, lwd = 2)


```

```{r}

col_virginica  <- "#d95f02"

dens_virginica  <- density(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "virginica"])

par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))

     xlim = range(d0$Petal.Width),

lines(dens_virginica, col = col_virginica, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

rug(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "versicolor"], col = paste0(col_versicolor, "99"))
rug(d0$Petal.Width[d0$Species == "virginica"], side = 3, col = paste0(col_virginica, "99"))

LDA assumes normality, and thus we would expect LDA model to be a good match when modelling species prediction using the width of petals. Notably the assumption is not needed when applying logistic regression. As @fig-chunk1 shows, both models yield approximately equal predictions. Over the considered range, the biggest difference in predicted probabilities between the models in 0.14.

xg <- seq(min(d$Petal.Width), max(d$Petal.Width), length.out = 400)

p_lda <- predict(lda_fit, newdata = data.frame(Petal.Width = xg))$posterior[, "virginica"]
p_glm <- predict(glm_fit, newdata = data.frame(Petal.Width = xg), type = "response")

# col_bayes <- "#7570b3"

plot(xg, p_lda, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_lda, yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Petal.Width", ylab = "P(virginica | Petal.Width)",
     main = "Predicted probability curves", ylim = c(0, 1))
lines(xg, p_glm, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = col_glm)
# lines(xg, p_bayes, lwd = 2, lty = 3, col = col_bayes)

## y-axis on [0,1], tick labels to 1 decimal place
y_ticks <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)
axis(2, at = y_ticks, labels = sprintf("%.1f", y_ticks), las = 1)

## Maximal gap between the two predicted curves, marked with a vertical
## segment capped by small horizontal ticks at each end (a "dimension line").
gap <- abs(p_lda - p_glm)
i_max <- which.max(gap)
x_max <- xg[i_max]

y_hi <- max(p_lda[i_max], p_glm[i_max])

legend("bottomright", bty = "n", legend = c("LDA", "Logistic regression"),
       col = c(col_lda, col_glm), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2))

## Right panel: reliability diagram, smooth form -- x-axis is the predicted
## probability from logistic regression, y-axis is the true (reference)
## probability from LDA. Both are evaluated on the same grid xg used in the
## left panel, so the curve is the parametric plot x -> (p_glm(x), p_lda(x));
## the dashed diagonal marks perfect agreement.
plot(p_glm, p_lda, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = col_glm,
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1,
     xlab = "Predicted P (logistic regression)",
     ylab = "True P (LDA)", main = "Reliability diagram")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey40")

## Same maximal gap as in the left panel (same index i_max into xg), shown
## here as the vertical distance from the curve to the diagonal at
## x = p_glm[i_max] -- i.e. from (p_glm[i_max], p_glm[i_max]) on the
## diagonal up to (p_glm[i_max], p_lda[i_max]) on the curve.
x0 <- p_glm[i_max]
arrows(x0 = x0, y0 = x0, x1 = x0, y1 = p_lda[i_max],
       code = 3, angle = 90, length = 0.05, lwd = 1.5, col = "black")
text(x0, (x0 + p_lda[i_max]) / 2, sprintf("max gap = %.2f", gap[i_max]), pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
```

Interestingly, we cannot carry out the comparison for virginica and setosa samples because the fitting procedure for logistic regression will not converge. Let us explain the reason. Logistic regression model is fitted by maximizing the likelihood on the dataset with features $\mathbf{x_i}$ and provided labels $y_i$. In our case $$
\overbrace{L(w, b)}^{\textrm{likelihood function}} = \prod_i \left\{ \sigma(wx_i + b)\ \ \ \ \mathrm{ when  }\ y_i = virginica \atop 1 - \sigma(wx_i + b)\ \mathrm{ when  }\ y_i = versicolor \right\}.
$$ The key fact is that the ranges of petal width do not intersect (the data is linearly separable), as seen from summary statistics for each species shown in @tbl-petalwidth. For any $\lambda > 0$ we have $$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda (x_i - 1) > 0 \quad y_i = virginica\\
\lambda (x_i - 1) < 0 \quad y_i = setosa
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-logistic3} Thus if we choose $w = \lambda$ and $b = -\lambda$ and let $\lambda \rightarrow \infty$, we see that $L(w, b)$ will approach 1 arbitrarily close. However it will never be exactly one, since for any $x$ the logistic function $\sigma(x) < 1$.

<!-- @tbl-petalwidth shows the range (minimum and maximum) of petal width for each of the three species. -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-petalwidth
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Summary statistics of Petal.Width (cm) by species
species_levels <- levels(iris$Species)
petal_width_tab <- data.frame(
  Species = species_levels,
  Count = sapply(species_levels, function(s) 
    sum(iris$Species == s)),
  Min  = sapply(species_levels, function(s) min(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  Max  = sapply(species_levels, function(s) max(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  Mean = sapply(species_levels, function(s) mean(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s])),
  SD   = sapply(species_levels, function(s) sd(iris$Petal.Width[iris$Species == s]))
)
## Two-line header only renders reliably in HTML; fall back to a plain
## single-line label for docx/jats so the pipe-table syntax isn't broken.
sd_label <- if (knitr::is_html_output()) "Standard<br>Deviation" else "Standard Deviation"
knitr::kable(petal_width_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Species", "Count", "Min", "Max", "Mean", sd_label))
```

<!-- Since the ranges do not intersect, it is possible to fit model so that probabilities at dataset points are arbitrarily close to the true values zero and one. -->

<!-- This problem does not occur with LDA. Let us recall that LDA model can be introduced one of two equivalent ways -->

<!-- -   by maximizing Fisher discriminant ratio for vector $\mathbf{w}$ as introduced, or -->

<!-- -   by maximum likelihood method where the parameters are the group means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and joint covariance matrix $\Sigma$ which form a generative model of data points $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$. -->

<!-- The first approach is considerably simpler. It is worth point out that although Fisher was a big proponent of maximum likelihood method, he eschewed maximum likelihood estimation and instead used the first approach when he introduced LDA [@fisher1936use]. The drawback of the first approach is that it does not directly yield $(\mathbf{w},b)$ in @eq-logistic. Instead it determines $\mathbf{w}$ up to a scalar multiple, since Fisher discriminant ratio is invariant to scaling of $\mathbf{w}$. -->

<!-- When using the first approach, the existence of the optimal $\mathbf{w}$ is assured by the fact that Fisher discriminant ratio is continuous in parameter $\mathbf{w}$ and is the same for any pair of collinear vectors. This allows to reduce the question to maximize the ratio on a sphere, which is a compact set, and thus a continuous function always attains maximum. -->

<!-- This argument would not work for logistic regression, since the objective, the expected likelihood $L(\mathbf{w}, b)$ is *not* invariant to rescaling the model's coefficients. -->

An observant reader may point out that we just need more samples. Indeed, Gaussian distribution has infinite support and thus under Gaussian assumption on class conditional densities, if we take enough samples, the ranges *will* intersect. The probability of the intersection can be computed exactly using order statistics. Suppose we draw $n$ samples per class, and let $F_s$, $F_v$, and $f_v$ denote the distribution functions of the two classes and the density of the second class. The setosa range $[\min_i X_i, \max_i X_i]$ fails to intersect the virginica range precisely when $\max_i X_i < \min_j Y_j$ (the reverse ordering has negligible probability, as setosa's mean lies far below virginica's). Conditioning on the position of the minimum $\min_j Y_j$, whose density is $n\,(1-F_v(t))^{n-1} f_v(t)$, and using independence of the two samples, $$
P\left(\max_i X_i < \min_j Y_j\right) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F_s(t)^n \; n\,\bigl(1-F_v(t)\bigr)^{n-1} f_v(t)\, dt.
$$ Evaluating this integral numerically with the plug-in parameters from @tbl-petalwidth (setosa: $\mu = 0.25$, $\sigma = 0.11$; virginica: $\mu = 2.03$, $\sigma = 0.27$) and solving for the sample size at which it drops to $1/2$ shows that one would need $n \approx 464\,000$ samples *per class* before the ranges have at least a 50% chance to intersect. The intuition for this enormous number is that the two means are more than six pooled standard deviations apart, so an intersection requires a joint extreme-tail event. Another modelling method is needed. We will introduce several alternatives next.

# Regularization of logistic regression

There are two principal paradigms to fit a logistic regression in the case of linear separation

-   applying prior on coefficients as typical in Bayesian statistics, or
-   extending Bernoulli model used in logistic regression to what we could call a *fractional Bernoulli model*.

In the first paradigm one uses the Bayes formula $$\textrm{posterior} \propto \textrm{likelihood}\times \textrm{prior}
$$ to replace maximization of log likelihood with $$
\max_{\mathbf{w}, b}  \log L(\mathbf{w},b)  + \log (\textrm{prior}(\mathbf{w})).
$$ There are several commonly used priors

-   L2 data dependent regularization, where the prior is the multivariate normal distribution; this method mirrors the classical Tikhonov's regularization [@tikhonov1963solution],
-   L1 data dependent regularization, where the prior is the multivariate Cauchy distribution [@friedman2010regularization]; this method encourages model's sparsity,
-   Firth logistic regression, where one uses Jeffrey's prior [@firth1993bias],
-   weakly informative Cauchy distribution proposed in [@gelman2008weakly],
-   multidimensional Student's $t$-distribution [@ghosh2018use].

The first two methods use crossvalidation to select the scale of the prior. The last two methods do not take the data into account, they only require that they are suitably transformed.

The second paradigm has been used in machine learning under names like Platt's scaling [@platt1999probabilistic] or label smoothing [@muller2019does]. In essence it enlarges the training dataset by replacing each sample in a group with label $y$ with $R$ samples with label $y$ and additional one sample with opposite label. This simple trick transforms a dataset with separable groups into a dataset where the two groups are inseparable. The way to choose $R$ is inspired by Laplace's (often ridiculed) work on calculating probability that the sun will rise tomorrow [@laplace1814essai]. It starts with a prior on probability and uses Bayes theorem to derive the posterior after a sequence of observed outcomes. Platt in his paper on probabilistic modelling for support vector machines used Laplace prior---the uniform prior on interval $[0,1]$. Somewhat overlooked was that Jeffrey's prior is a natural alternative. @tbl-prior-r summarizes the two choices, the value of $R$ each implies, and the name we use for the resulting method throughout the rest of the paper.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prior-r
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Two scaling (label smoothing) methods for logistic regression
prior_tab <- data.frame(
  Prior      = c("Laplace (uniform)", "Jeffreys"),
  Beta_prior = c("Beta(1, 1)", "Beta(1/2, 1/2)"),
  R          = c("$N + 1$", "$2N+1$"),
  Method     = c("Platt scaling", "SAH scaling [@such2025canonical]")
)
knitr::kable(prior_tab, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Prior", "Prior", "$R$", "Method name"))
```

Let us compare the predictions of these models. We shall apply them to a simulated data sets where we draw 50 samples from two normal distributions with unit variance and means at distance six. Since we generated the data, we can also include Bayes classifier. The results are shown in @fig-one-dataset-predictions. We can see that all models found the optimal separation point which lies midway between the means. However, they do differ significantly with LDA and data dependent L1 being closest to the Bayes classifier. The first is unsurprising, since our generative model matches exactly the assumption of LDA, but the latter is not expected.

```{r}
#| label: fig-one-dataset-predictions
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Predicted P(class B | x) from each of the eight models, together with the true Bayes-optimal probability, for a single simulated dataset (the first of the M Monte Carlo replications used in @fig-calibration-ratios below). Tick marks along the bottom show the sampled class A (dark) and class B (light) points.
#| fig-pos: 'H'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(glmnet)
  library(logistf)
  library(arm)
})

set.seed(1)   # same seed as simulate_calibration_ratios.R -> reproduces its first replication
n   <- 50
mu1 <- 0; mu2 <- 6; sdv <- 1

x1 <- rnorm(n, mu1, sdv)
x2 <- rnorm(n, mu2, sdv)
x  <- c(x1, x2)
y  <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = n))
yb <- as.integer(y == "B")

xg <- seq(min(x) - 1, max(x) + 1, length.out = 400)

## True Bayes-optimal probability curve (same closed form as in
## simulate_calibration_ratios.R).
b_true <- (mu2 - mu1) / sdv^2
a_true <- -(mu2^2 - mu1^2) / (2 * sdv^2)
p_true <- plogis(a_true + b_true * xg)

## L1 / L2 penalized logistic regression.
x_mean <- mean(x); x_sd <- sd(x)
X  <- cbind((x  - x_mean) / x_sd, 0)
Xg <- cbind((xg - x_mean) / x_sd, 0)
cv_l2 <- cv.glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, standardize = FALSE)
cv_l1 <- cv.glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, standardize = FALSE)
p_l2 <- as.numeric(predict(cv_l2, newx = Xg, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
p_l1 <- as.numeric(predict(cv_l1, newx = Xg, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))

## Firth logistic regression.
firth_fit <- logistf(yb ~ x, pl = FALSE)
p_firth <- plogis(coef(firth_fit)[1] + coef(firth_fit)[2] * xg)

## Platt scaling (standard and 2N-target variant).
Np <- sum(yb == 1); Nn <- sum(yb == 0)
t_std <- ifelse(yb == 1, (Np + 1) / (Np + 2), 1 / (Nn + 2))
t_2N  <- ifelse(yb == 1, (2 * Np + 1) / (2 * Np + 2), 1 / (2 * Nn + 2))
p_platt  <- predict(suppressWarnings(glm(t_std ~ x, family = binomial)),
                     newdata = data.frame(x = xg), type = "response")
p_platt2 <- predict(suppressWarnings(glm(t_2N ~ x, family = binomial)),
                     newdata = data.frame(x = xg), type = "response")

## LDA (pooled-variance closed form, as in simulate_calibration_ratios.R).
m1 <- mean(x1); m2 <- mean(x2)
s2_pooled <- ((n - 1) * var(x1) + (n - 1) * var(x2)) / (2 * n - 2)
b_lda <- (m2 - m1) / s2_pooled
a_lda <- -(m2^2 - m1^2) / (2 * s2_pooled)
p_lda <- plogis(a_lda + b_lda * xg)

## Bayesian logistic regression, posterior mode via arm::bayesglm, with
## Gelman et al.'s (2008) data-independent weakly informative priors:
## Cauchy(0, 2.5) (prior.df = 1), and a Student-t (df = 4) variant.
cauchy_fit <- bayesglm(yb ~ x, family = binomial,
                       prior.scale = 2.5, prior.df = 1,
                       prior.scale.for.intercept = 10,
                       prior.df.for.intercept = 1)
p_cauchy <- plogis(coef(cauchy_fit)[1] + coef(cauchy_fit)[2] * xg)

t_fit <- bayesglm(yb ~ x, family = binomial,
                  prior.scale = 2.5, prior.df = 4,
                  prior.scale.for.intercept = 10,
                  prior.df.for.intercept = 4)

```

<!-- To compare how well each regularized model recovers the true class probability, we ran a Monte Carlo simulation with $M=`r M_reps`$ replications: repeatedly sampling $N=50$ points per class from two unit-variance normal distributions with means 6 apart, fitting L1-penalized logistic regression, L2-penalized logistic regression, Firth logistic regression, Platt scaling, Platt scaling with halved pseudocounts ("2N" targets), LDA, and Bayesian logistic regression (posterior mode) under two data-independent weakly informative priors — the Cauchy(0, 2.5) default of Gelman et al. (2008) and a lighter-tailed Student-$t_7$(0, 2.5) variant — to each sample, and recording, at every sampled point, the ratio of each model's predicted to the true (Bayes-optimal) probability of being class B. Unlike Firth's Jeffreys-prior penalty, which depends on the design matrix, both weakly informative priors are fixed in advance; the Cauchy's heavy tails let strongly informative data override the prior, while the $t_7$ shrinks large coefficients more aggressively. @fig-one-dataset-predictions shows what a single replication looks like: the predicted-probability curve from each of the eight models, together with the true Bayes curve, fitted to one simulated dataset. @fig-calibration-ratios then shows the resulting distribution of $\log_{10}(\hat{p}/p_{\text{true}})$ for each method, restricted to points sampled from class A; a value of 0 indicates perfect calibration at that point, positive values indicate the model overestimated the true probability, and negative values indicate underestimation. We restrict to class-A points because $p_{\text{true}}$ is bounded away from $1$ there: class A sits 6 SDs from class B, so $p_{\text{true}}$ only approaches $1$ for a class-A point that is itself several SDs from its own mean, which essentially never happens. Class-B points, by contrast, almost always have $p_{\text{true}} \approx 1$, where $\log p$ is insensitive to the model's actual log-odds and the ratio is uninformative regardless of how wrong the model is. Nothing is lost by dropping class-B points: the whole setup — both Gaussians and all eight fitting procedures — is symmetric under swapping the class labels and reflecting $x$ about the midpoint, so class-A and class-B behavior are mirror images in distribution. Because the two class means are 6 SDs apart, the two classes end up linearly separable in $x$ (some threshold perfectly splits class A from class B) in the large majority of replications; in that regime, weakly-regularized models can drive predicted probabilities toward 0/1, showing up here as strongly negative log-ratios. -->

We now investigate whether this dissimilarity persists in repeated simulations. We evaluate ratio of predicted probability to true probability (on log scale) for 30 replications for each data point in class A. The results are shown in @fig-calibration-ratios. All variants of logistic regression show consistent overconfidence in their predictions, most with more than five (!) orders of magnitude. The only exceptions are data dependent L1 regression (mean = 1.5) and regression using weakly informative Cauchy prior (mean = 4.3). We refer to this suprising strong overconfidence as *multiplicative miscalibration*. The adjective multiplicative refers to the fact that absolute difference in two probabilities is minuscule, it is the *ratio of probabilities* that is consistenly very large.

```{r}
#| label: fig-calibration-ratios
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Distribution of log10(predicted probability / true probability) for each regularization method, restricted to class-A points and pooled across all Monte Carlo replications. The dashed red line marks perfect calibration (ratio = 1).
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
model_order  <- c("L1", "L2", "Firth", "Platt", "Platt_2N", "LDA",
                  "Cauchy", "StudentT")
model_labels <- c(L1 = "data dependent L1", L2 = "data dependent L2", Firth = "Firth logistic",
                  Platt = "Platt scaling", Platt_2N = "SAH scaling", LDA = "LDA",
                  Cauchy = "Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior", StudentT = "Student-t(4) prior")

par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1),
    cex.axis = 1.2, cex.lab = 1.25, cex.main = 1.3)
for (m in model_order) {
  log_ratio <- ratios_df$log10_ratio[ratios_df$model == m & ratios_df$class == "A"]
  h <- hist(log_ratio, breaks = 40, plot = FALSE)
  ymax <- max(h$density) * 1.15

  hist(log_ratio, breaks = h$breaks, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white",
       xlab = "log10(predicted prob / true prob)", ylab = "Density", ylim = c(0, ymax),
       main = unname(model_labels[m]), yaxt = "n")
  axis(2, labels = FALSE)
  abline(v = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

  ## Small downward arrow at the mean, roughly mid-height, labeled above it.
  m_val <- mean(log_ratio)
  y_top <- ymax * 0.65
  y_bot <- ymax * 0.45
  arrows(x0 = m_val, y0 = y_top, x1 = m_val, y1 = y_bot,
         col = "blue", lwd = 2, length = 0.08)
  text(m_val, y_top, sprintf("mean=%.1f", m_val), col = "blue", pos = 3, cex = 1.4)
}
```

![Multiplicative miscalibration of Firth logistic regression as a function of class separation. For each Cohen's *d* between 1 and 8, 100 datasets of 50 samples per class were drawn from N(0,1) and N(*d*,1), and the predicted probability of the less likely class was evaluated at the mode of class A (*x* = 0). The purple curve shows the mean of log10(predicted probability / true probability) with a ±1 sd band; the dashed red line marks perfect calibration. The top axis gives the true odds ratio per 1 SD of *x* corresponding to each *d*, and the right axis (log scale) shows the true OR = exp(*d*) (dotted black) alongside the mean Firth-fitted OR (green). Miscalibration is negligible up to *d* ≈ 3.5 and takes off where samples of this size become frequently linearly separable; past that threshold the fitted OR flattens and declines while the true OR keeps growing, so the two curves are complementary views of the same information loss.](firth_dscan.png){#fig-firth-dscan}

# Applications

Let us describe three applications which could by affected by the phenomenon of multiplicative miscalibration.

## Risk assessment of low probability events

In financial markets, as well as in insurance industry, it is paramount to properly estimate risk. Since one can generally choose to either to buy or to sell a financial instrument (stock, bond, or credit-default swap), an incorrectly set price--both too high or too low---of the instrument provides an opportunity for profiting without taking any risk. The biggest potential payoff is in prediction of very rare events, which typically correspond to highly separable group distributions. Logistic regression is widely used to estimate risk of rare events [@ogundimu2019prediction]. We have seen that multiplicative miscalibration may occur at several orders of magnitude, and thus could provide fabulous returns to a savvy investor if he spots it. Of course, open markets would eventually self-correct and diminish such investment opening. Nevertheless, the first-mover would enjoy a one-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

## Partial one-vs-one classification

```{r}
#| label: partial-coupling-setup
#| include: false
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Partial one-vs-one coupling on speaker embeddings: both English fables,
## 400 ms non-overlapping clips, each recording split 70/30 in time (first 70 %
## of its speech -> training, last 30 % -> testing) before cutting.
## Embeddings: prepare_embeddings.py --seg-ms 400 --overlap 0 --audio-split 0.7
## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
EMB_CSV <- "data/embeddings_EN_EB_400ms_overlap0_audiosplit70.csv"
if (!file.exists(EMB_CSV)) {
  ## First render on a new machine: build the embeddings from recordings/ with
  ## prepare_embeddings.py. Unless AMS_PYTHON points to a Python that already has
  ## the packages in requirements.txt, a local environment .venv is created and
  ## the packages are installed into it (needs Python 3.9-3.12 and internet;
  ## a few minutes and about 1 GB once). Later renders reuse the CSV.
  venv_py <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") file.path(".venv", "Scripts", "python.exe") else file.path(".venv", "bin", "python")
  py <- Sys.getenv("AMS_PYTHON", unset = "")
  if (!nzchar(py)) {
    if (!file.exists(venv_py)) {
      sys_py <- Sys.which(c("python3", "python"))
      sys_py <- unname(sys_py[nzchar(sys_py)][1])
      if (is.na(sys_py)) stop("Python 3 is needed to prepare the speaker embeddings (https://www.python.org).")
      stopifnot(system2(sys_py, c("-m", "venv", ".venv")) == 0)
      stopifnot(system2(venv_py, c("-m", "pip", "install", "--upgrade", "pip")) == 0)
      stopifnot(system2(venv_py, c("-m", "pip", "install", "-r", "requirements.txt")) == 0)
    }
    py <- venv_py
  }
  status <- system2(py, c("prepare_embeddings.py", "--seg-ms", "400", "--overlap", "0", "--audio-split", "0.7"))
  stopifnot(status == 0, file.exists(EMB_CSV))
}
emb <- read.csv(EMB_CSV)
emb$speaker <- factor(emb$speaker)
X192 <- as.matrix(emb[, grep("^dim_", names(emb))])
spk  <- levels(emb$speaker)                                    # "A" "M" "S"
is_train <- emb$set == "train"
Xtr192 <- X192[is_train, ];  ytr <- emb$speaker[is_train]
Xte192 <- X192[!is_train, ]; yte <- emb$speaker[!is_train]
p192 <- ncol(X192); K3 <- 3
n_tr <- nrow(Xtr192); n_te <- nrow(Xte192)

## Regularized LDA projection 192 -> K-1 = 2, fitted on the training data only.
## S_w is shrunk toward a scaled identity before inversion because n only
## moderately exceeds p; whitening then makes the pooled within-class covariance
## spherical.
alpha3 <- 0.5
nk3    <- as.integer(table(ytr))
mu192  <- t(sapply(spk, function(k) colMeans(Xtr192[ytr == k, ])))
Sw192  <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(1:K3, function(i)
            (nk3[i] - 1) * cov(Xtr192[ytr == spk[i], ]))) / (nrow(Xtr192) - K3)
Sw192  <- (1 - alpha3) * Sw192 + alpha3 * mean(diag(Sw192)) * diag(p192)
ew192  <- eigen(Sw192, symmetric = TRUE)
Wh192  <- ew192$vectors %*% diag(1 / sqrt(pmax(ew192$values, 1e-12))) %*% t(ew192$vectors)
V2     <- eigen(cov(mu192 %*% Wh192) * (K3 - 1), symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[, 1:2]
P2     <- Wh192 %*% V2

Ztr <- Xtr192 %*% P2; Zte <- Xte192 %*% P2
means3 <- t(sapply(spk, function(k) colMeans(Ztr[ytr == k, ])))
dimnames(means3) <- list(spk, c("x", "y"))
dat3  <- data.frame(x = Ztr[, 1], y = Ztr[, 2], class = ytr)   # training
test3 <- data.frame(x = Zte[, 1], y = Zte[, 2], class = yte)   # test, plotted

## ---- properties of the reduced data (as in assumption_checks.R) -----------
royston_H <- function(X) {
  X <- as.matrix(X); n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
  kurt <- function(v) { m <- mean(v); mean((v - m)^4) / mean((v - m)^2)^2 }
  sf_W <- function(v) cor(sort(v), qnorm(ppoints(length(v), a = 3/8)))^2
  lx <- log(n)
  mu <- -1.5861 - 0.31082 * lx - 0.083751 * lx^2 + 0.0038915 * lx^3
  sg <- exp(-0.4803 - 0.082676 * lx + 0.0030302 * lx^2)
  z <- vapply(seq_len(p), function(i) {
    v <- X[, i]
    W <- if (kurt(v) > 3) sf_W(v) else as.numeric(shapiro.test(v)$statistic)
    (log(1 - W) - mu) / sg
  }, numeric(1))
  u <- 0.715; v <- 0.21364 + 0.015124 * lx^2 - 0.0018034 * lx^3; l <- 5
  C  <- cor(X); NC <- (C^l) * (1 - (u * (1 - C)^u) / v)
  mC <- (sum(NC) - p) / (p^2 - p); edf <- p / (1 + (p - 1) * mC)
  H  <- edf * sum(qnorm(pnorm(-z) / 2)^2) / p
  pchisq(H, df = edf, lower.tail = FALSE)
}
box_M <- function(Z, g) {
  lv <- levels(droplevels(g)); gq <- length(lv); m <- nrow(Z); q <- ncol(Z)
  ni <- as.integer(table(g)[lv])
  Si <- lapply(lv, function(k) cov(Z[g == k, , drop = FALSE]))
  Sp <- Reduce(`+`, Map(function(S, a) (a - 1) * S, Si, ni)) / (m - gq)
  M  <- (m - gq) * log(det(Sp)) - sum((ni - 1) * sapply(Si, function(S) log(det(S))))
  c1 <- (sum(1 / (ni - 1)) - 1 / (m - gq)) * (2 * q^2 + 3 * q - 1) / (6 * (q + 1) * (gq - 1))
  pchisq(M * (1 - c1), (gq - 1) * q * (q + 1) / 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
}
mahalanobis_dist <- function(Z, g, a, b) {
  i <- g == a; j <- g == b
  S  <- ((sum(i) - 1) * cov(Z[i, ]) + (sum(j) - 1) * cov(Z[j, ])) / (sum(i) + sum(j) - 2)
  dm <- colMeans(Z[i, ]) - colMeans(Z[j, ])
  sqrt(as.numeric(t(dm) %*% solve(S) %*% dm))
}
separable_pair <- function(Z, g, a, b) {
  idx <- g %in% c(a, b); yy <- as.integer(g[idx] == b)
  fit <- suppressWarnings(glm(yy ~ Z[idx, ], family = binomial))
  all((fitted(fit) > 0.5) == (yy == 1))
}
roy_tr <- sapply(spk, function(k) royston_H(Ztr[ytr == k, ]))
roy_te <- sapply(spk, function(k) royston_H(Zte[yte == k, ]))
boxM_tr <- box_M(Ztr, ytr); boxM_te <- box_M(Zte, yte)
pair_names <- sapply(combn(spk, 2, simplify = FALSE), paste, collapse = "-")
d_tr <- setNames(sapply(combn(spk, 2, simplify = FALSE), function(pr) mahalanobis_dist(Ztr, ytr, pr[1], pr[2])), pair_names)
d_te <- setNames(sapply(combn(spk, 2, simplify = FALSE), function(pr) mahalanobis_dist(Zte, yte, pr[1], pr[2])), pair_names)
sep_tr <- setNames(sapply(combn(spk, 2, simplify = FALSE), function(pr) separable_pair(Ztr, ytr, pr[1], pr[2])), pair_names)
sep_te <- setNames(sapply(combn(spk, 2, simplify = FALSE), function(pr) separable_pair(Zte, yte, pr[1], pr[2])), pair_names)

pairs3 <- combn(3, 2, simplify = FALSE)   # (1,2) (1,3) (2,3) indexing spk

## LDA pairwise fits: closed-form pooled-covariance discriminant, evaluated
## as a raw linear score (not via predict.lda) so it stays informative at
## full precision far from the training data.
lda_pair_coef <- list()
for (pr in pairs3) {
  lo <- pr[1]; hi <- pr[2]
  Xlo <- as.matrix(dat3[as.integer(dat3$class) == lo, c("x", "y")])
  Xhi <- as.matrix(dat3[as.integer(dat3$class) == hi, c("x", "y")])
  n_lo <- nrow(Xlo); n_hi <- nrow(Xhi)
  mlo <- colMeans(Xlo); mhi <- colMeans(Xhi)
  Sigma <- ((n_lo - 1) * cov(Xlo) + (n_hi - 1) * cov(Xhi)) / (n_lo + n_hi - 2)
  Sinv  <- solve(Sigma)
  w <- as.numeric(Sinv %*% (mhi - mlo))
  b <- -0.5 * as.numeric(mhi %*% Sinv %*% mhi - mlo %*% Sinv %*% mlo) + log(n_hi / n_lo)
  lda_pair_coef[[paste0(lo, "_", hi)]] <- list(w = w, b = b)
}
lda_eta_pair_raw <- function(lo, hi, Xnew) {
  cf <- lda_pair_coef[[paste0(lo, "_", hi)]]
  as.numeric(Xnew %*% cf$w + cf$b)
}

## Firth pairwise fits (bias-reduced logistic regression via modified-score
## IRLS), evaluated as a raw linear predictor for the same reason.
firth_logistic3 <- function(X, y, tol = 1e-8, max_iter = 200) {
  X <- cbind(Intercept = 1, X)
  beta <- rep(0, ncol(X))
  for (i in 1:max_iter) {
    eta  <- as.vector(X %*% beta)
    p_i  <- plogis(eta)
    W    <- p_i * (1 - p_i)
    XtWX <- t(X) %*% (X * W)
    XtWX_inv <- solve(XtWX)
    h <- W * rowSums((X %*% XtWX_inv) * X)
    U_star <- t(X) %*% (y - p_i + h * (0.5 - p_i))
    step <- as.vector(XtWX_inv %*% U_star)
    beta <- beta + step
    if (max(abs(step)) < tol) break
  }
  list(beta = beta)
}
firth_pair_fits <- list()
for (pr in pairs3) {
  lo <- pr[1]; hi <- pr[2]
  sub <- dat3[as.integer(dat3$class) %in% c(lo, hi), ]
  Xp <- as.matrix(sub[, c("x", "y")])
  yp <- as.integer(as.integer(sub$class) == hi)
  firth_pair_fits[[paste0(lo, "_", hi)]] <- firth_logistic3(Xp, yp)
}
firth_eta_pair_raw <- function(lo, hi, Xnew) {
  fit <- firth_pair_fits[[paste0(lo, "_", hi)]]
  as.numeric(cbind(1, Xnew) %*% fit$beta)
}

## Signed log-odds of class a over class b (a != b, either order), for a
## given base classifier's raw pairwise score function.
make_log_odds <- function(eta_pair_raw) {
  function(a, b, Xnew) {
    lo <- min(a, b); hi <- max(a, b)
    eta <- eta_pair_raw(lo, hi, Xnew)
    if (a == hi) eta else -eta
  }
}
lda_log_odds   <- make_log_odds(lda_eta_pair_raw)
firth_log_odds <- make_log_odds(firth_eta_pair_raw)

## Closed-form partial WLW coupling: p_i : p_j : p_k = exp(eta_ik) : exp(eta_jk) : 1,
## computed via the standard softmax stabilization from the never-saturated
## raw log-odds (see prose).
couple_predict_partial <- function(Xnew, i, j, k, log_odds_fn) {
  eta_i <- log_odds_fn(i, k, Xnew)
  eta_j <- log_odds_fn(j, k, Xnew)
  L <- matrix(0, nrow(Xnew), 3)
  L[, i] <- eta_i; L[, j] <- eta_j; L[, k] <- 0
  w <- exp(L - apply(L, 1, max))
  w / rowSums(w)
}

## Full (3-term) WLW coupling via the Wu-Lin-Weng (2004) fixed-point iteration.
wlw_couple <- function(r, max_iter = 200, eps = 0.005 / nrow(r)) {
  k <- nrow(r); Q <- matrix(0, k, k)
  for (pr in pairs3) {
    a <- pr[1]; b <- pr[2]
    Q[a, a] <- Q[a, a] + r[b, a]^2; Q[b, b] <- Q[b, b] + r[a, b]^2
    Q[a, b] <- Q[a, b] - r[b, a] * r[a, b]; Q[b, a] <- Q[b, a] - r[a, b] * r[b, a]
  }
  p <- rep(1 / k, k)
  for (iter in 1:max_iter) {
    Qp <- as.vector(Q %*% p); pQp <- sum(p * Qp)
    if (max(abs(Qp - pQp)) < eps) break
    for (t in 1:k) {
      diff <- (-Qp[t] + pQp) / Q[t, t]
      p[t] <- p[t] + diff
      pQp  <- (pQp + diff * (diff * Q[t, t] + 2 * Qp[t])) / (1 + diff)^2
      Qp   <- (Qp + diff * Q[t, ]) / (1 + diff)
      p    <- p / (1 + diff)
    }
  }
  p / sum(p)
}
couple_predict_full <- function(Xnew, log_odds_fn) {
  R <- lapply(1:3, function(a) lapply(1:3, function(b)
         if (a == b) rep(0, nrow(Xnew)) else plogis(log_odds_fn(a, b, Xnew))))
  t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(Xnew)), function(row) {
    r <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
    for (a in 1:3) for (b in 1:3) r[a, b] <- R[[a]][[b]][row]
    wlw_couple(r)
  }))
}

## Plug-in Bayes-optimal classifier from the ESTIMATED class means. The plane is
## sphered, so with equal priors this is the nearest-mean rule.
bayes_predict3 <- function(Xnew) {
  D <- sapply(1:3, function(k)
        rowSums((Xnew - matrix(means3[k, ], nrow(Xnew), 2, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  logf <- -0.5 * D
  ex <- exp(logf - apply(logf, 1, max))
  ex / rowSums(ex)
}

drops <- list(drop12 = c(i = 1, j = 2, k = 3),
              drop13 = c(i = 1, j = 3, k = 2),
              drop23 = c(i = 2, j = 3, k = 1))
drop_titles <- c(drop12 = sprintf("drop pair (%s,%s)", spk[1], spk[2]),
                 drop13 = sprintf("drop pair (%s,%s)", spk[1], spk[3]),
                 drop23 = sprintf("drop pair (%s,%s)", spk[2], spk[3]))

## ---- held-out accuracies ----------------------------------------------------
Xte2  <- as.matrix(test3[, c("x", "y")])
truth <- as.integer(test3$class)
acc <- function(P) mean(max.col(P) == truth)
acc_bayes <- acc(bayes_predict3(Xte2))
acc_full  <- c(LDA = acc(couple_predict_full(Xte2, lda_log_odds)),
               Firth = acc(couple_predict_full(Xte2, firth_log_odds)))
acc_drop  <- sapply(drops, function(d) c(
  LDA   = acc(couple_predict_partial(Xte2, d[["i"]], d[["j"]], d[["k"]], lda_log_odds)),
  Firth = acc(couple_predict_partial(Xte2, d[["i"]], d[["j"]], d[["k"]], firth_log_odds))))
lda_max_change <- max(abs(acc_drop["LDA", ] - acc_full["LDA"]))
pred_dropAS <- max.col(couple_predict_partial(Xte2, 1, 3, 2, firth_log_odds))
n_S_to_A <- sum(truth == 3 & pred_dropAS == 1)

## ---- linkage-class miscalibration (fig-miscal-box) -----------------------
## log10 p(k | x) from the pairwise classifier of pair (c, k), computed on the
## log scale from the raw log-odds, so no clamping is needed.
log10_pk <- function(c, k, X, eta_fn) {
  lo <- min(c, k); hi <- max(c, k)
  sgn <- if (k == hi) 1 else -1                      # log-odds of k over c
  plogis(sgn * eta_fn(lo, hi, X), log.p = TRUE) / log(10)
}
## For each dropped pair (i, j) with linkage class k: classifier i-k on the
## class-i test points and classifier j-k on the class-j test points.
link <- list(); link_diff <- numeric(0); link_lab <- character(0); link_acc <- numeric(0)
for (d in drops) {
  i <- d[["i"]]; j <- d[["j"]]; k <- d[["k"]]
  for (c in c(i, j)) {
    X <- Xte2[truth == c, , drop = FALSE]
    link[[length(link) + 1]] <- list(
      v = log10_pk(c, k, X, firth_eta_pair_raw) - log10_pk(c, k, X, lda_eta_pair_raw),
      cls = c, lab = sprintf("%s-%s\n(%s points)", spk[c], spk[k], spk[c]))
  }
  n <- length(link)
  link_diff <- c(link_diff, median(link[[n]]$v) - median(link[[n - 1]]$v))
  link_lab  <- c(link_lab, sprintf("drop %s-%s (linkage %s)", spk[i], spk[j], spk[k]))
  sel <- truth %in% c(i, j)      # accuracy on the test clips of the two dropped classes
  link_acc  <- c(link_acc, mean(max.col(couple_predict_partial(Xte2[sel, ], i, j, k, firth_log_odds)) == truth[sel]))
}
names(link_diff) <- names(link_acc) <- names(drops)

f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
```

The models discussed so far are inherently binary. A common way to extend a binary classifier to $K > 2$ classes is to fit a model on every pair of classes and then *couple* the $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise probability estimates into a single probability vector over all $K$ classes [@hastie1998classification]. There have been many proposals of coupling methods, but the one in most common use was proposed by Wu--Lin--Weng [@wu2004probability].

We empirically evaluate the pairwise coupling framework using a three-class ($K = 3$) speaker recognition task. The dataset includes speech audio from three speakers ($A$, $M$, and $S$), each reciting two English fables: *The North Wind and the Sun* and *The Boy Who Cried Wolf*. The process of converting the raw recordings into classifier-ready inputs follows a short pipeline. First, the audio is resampled to 16 kHz. An energy-based voice-activity detection method retains only segments that are predominantly speech, removing silence and background noise. The first 70% of each speaker's audio is used for training and the last 30% for testing. Inside each part separately, the audio is segmented into non-overlapping 400 ms clips. Each clip is processed by a pretrained speaker-embedding neural network, ECAPA-TDNN [@desplanques2020ecapa], which compresses it into a 192-dimensional vector that summarizes speaker identity, independent of spoken content. Each embedding is subsequently re-scaled to unit $L_2$ norm. This yields $N_{\text{train}} = `r n_tr`$ training embedding vectors (`r n_tr / K3` per speaker) and $N_{\text{test}} = `r n_te`$ test embedding vectors (`r n_te / K3` per speaker).

In order to reduce the `r p192`-dimensional embedding space to $K-1=2$ canonical discriminant directions, we use regularized linear discriminant analysis [@friedman1989regularized]. Since the training sample size ($N_{\text{train}} = `r n_tr`$) is only moderately larger than the number of features ($p = `r p192`$), the empirical pooled within-class covariance matrix is ill-conditioned. To overcome this, we apply linear covariance shrinkage towards a scaled identity with a shrinkage intensity of $\gamma = `r alpha3`$. The projection is fitted on the training points only and then applied unchanged to the test points; in the resulting two-dimensional whitened projection the training data's pooled within-class covariance matrix is sphered. The reduced-dimensional data have the following properties:

1. Each class approximately follows a bivariate normal distribution with a shared covariance matrix. On the training set, Royston's multivariate Shapiro--Wilk test [@royston1983some] indicates no significant deviation from normality for any speaker (smallest $p = `r f3(min(roy_tr))`$); on the test set it detects modest departures for speakers $A$ and $S$ ($p = `r f3(roy_te[["A"]])`$ and $p = `r f3(roy_te[["S"]])`$). Box's $M$ test [@friendly2020visualizing] fails to reject the null hypothesis of equal class covariances on either set ($p = `r f3(boxM_tr)`$ and $p = `r f3(boxM_te)`$).
2. Under homoscedastic bivariate normal distributions, the nearest-sample-mean rule constitutes the plug-in Bayes-optimal decision boundary---the dashed line overlaid in @fig-partial-coupling below.
3. All class pairs are perfectly linearly separable in the training set. The Mahalanobis distances $\Delta$ between the class means (the multivariate generalisation of Cohen's $d$, to which $\Delta$ reduces in one dimension) for the pairs ($A$--$M$, $A$--$S$, $M$--$S$) are $`r f2(d_tr[["A-M"]])`$, $`r f2(d_tr[["A-S"]])`$, and $`r f2(d_tr[["M-S"]])`$ on the training set, and $`r f2(d_te[["A-M"]])`$, $`r f2(d_te[["A-S"]])`$, and $`r f2(d_te[["M-S"]])`$ on the test set, where only the pair $M$--$S$ remains separable. The training distances are larger because the projection was fitted on the training clips.

To evaluate model generalization for each pair of classes, we fit two different one-vs-one base classifiers: LDA (closed-form pooled-covariance discriminant) and a Firth (bias-reduced) logistic regression [@firth1993bias], the latter generalizing the one-dimensional Firth fit used earlier in this paper. For each base classifier, the three pairwise fits are combined into one three-class probability vector via the fixed-point iteration of Wu, Lin and Weng (2004)---the same algorithm LIBSVM uses to turn one-vs-one SVM outputs into multi-class probabilities [@chang2011libsvm]. Full (3-term) WLW coupling recovers the Bayes decision boundaries closely for both base classifiers: on the held-out points, LDA and Firth reach accuracies of $`r f3(acc_full[["LDA"]])`$ and $`r f3(acc_full[["Firth"]])`$, against $`r f3(acc_bayes)`$ for the plug-in Bayes classifier.

Wu--Lin--Weng coupling finds the probability vector $p$ minimizing $L(p) = \sum_{i<j}(r_{ji}\,p_i - r_{ij}\,p_j)^2$, a sum over all $\binom{3}{2}=3$ pairwise terms, where $r_{ij}$ is the pairwise estimate of the probability of class $i$ given that the point belongs to class $i$ or $j$.

With only three classes, dropping pair $(i,j)$ leaves exactly two terms in the objective, for pairs $(i,k)$ and $(j,k)$ with $k$ the remaining class. These two terms are independent of each other (neither involves both $p_i$ and $p_j$), so both can be driven to exactly zero at once: $r_{ki}\,p_i = r_{ik}\,p_k$ and $r_{kj}\,p_j = r_{jk}\,p_k$. This pins down the class ratios directly from the two kept pairwise odds, $p_i:p_j:p_k = \frac{r_{ik}}{r_{ki}} : \frac{r_{jk}}{r_{kj}} : 1$, with no optimization needed at all. We evaluate this ratio from each pairwise classifier's raw log-odds rather than from its probability output: with class means $`r f2(min(d_tr))`$--$`r f2(max(d_tr))`$ units apart, a pairwise probability routinely saturates to exactly $0$ or $1$ in floating point, which would silently discard precisely the information needed to tell $i$ and $j$ apart far from class $k$.

@fig-partial-coupling shows the argmax regions for all three partial-coupling variants (rows) using LDA (left column) and Firth logistic regression (right column) as the one-vs-one base classifier. Dropping the pair $(i,j)$ predictably degrades the boundary specifically between classes $i$ and $j$ (since the coupling step no longer sees that pairwise comparison directly, only indirectly through their shared comparisons with class $k$), while leaving the region boundaries involving the third class comparatively unaffected. The two base classifiers differ sharply in how much damage this causes, however: LDA's decision regions move only slightly under all three pair removals (its accuracy changes by at most $`r round(100 * lda_max_change)`$ percentage points), while Firth's shift markedly and collapse for one specific dropped pair---dropping $(A,S)$ reduces Firth's held-out accuracy from $`r f3(acc_full[["Firth"]])`$ to $`r f3(acc_drop["Firth", "drop13"])`$, with $`r n_S_to_A`$ of the $`r sum(truth == 3)`$ test points of speaker $S$ assigned to speaker $A$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-partial-coupling
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: Argmax decision regions under partial (2-term) Wu--Lin--Weng coupling on the three-speaker dataset, dropping one pairwise term at a time (rows), for LDA (left column) and Firth logistic regression (right column) as the one-vs-one base classifier. Points are the held-out test clips, crosses the training class means. The plug-in Bayes boundary is overlaid (dashed).
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 10.5

## Grid over the rectangle bounding the data and the three means.
margin3 <- 4
allxy <- rbind(as.matrix(dat3[, c("x","y")]), as.matrix(test3[, c("x","y")]), means3)
gx3 <- seq(min(allxy[, 1]) - margin3, max(allxy[, 1]) + margin3, length.out = 200)
gy3 <- seq(min(allxy[, 2]) - margin3, max(allxy[, 2]) + margin3, length.out = 200)
grid3 <- expand.grid(x = gx3, y = gy3)
Xg3 <- as.matrix(grid3)
nx3 <- length(gx3); ny3 <- length(gy3)
grid3$pred_bayes <- max.col(bayes_predict3(Xg3))

class_cols3 <- c("#e41a1c", "#4daf4a", "#377eb8")   # red, green, blue

add_bayes_boundary3 <- function() {
  contour(gx3, gy3, matrix(grid3$pred_bayes, nx3, ny3), levels = c(1.5, 2.5),
          add = TRUE, drawlabels = FALSE, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "black")
}

## Points shown are the held-out test clips; the crosses are the training
## centroids that define the plug-in Bayes boundary.
plot_argmax_panel <- function(pred_col, title) {
  image(gx3, gy3, matrix(pred_col, nx3, ny3),
        col = adjustcolor(class_cols3, alpha.f = 0.15), breaks = c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5),
        xlab = "", ylab = "", asp = 1, main = title, useRaster = TRUE)
  points(test3$x, test3$y, col = class_cols3[as.integer(test3$class)], pch = 16, cex = 0.4)
  points(means3[, 1], means3[, 2], pch = 4, lwd = 3, cex = 1.3)
  add_bayes_boundary3()
}

## Layout: a slim legend row spanning both columns on top, then the 3x2
## grid of panels below.
layout(matrix(c(1, 1,
                2, 3,
                4, 5,
                6, 7), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE),
       heights = c(0.6, 3, 3, 3))

par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend("center", bty = "n", cex = 1.4, horiz = TRUE,
       legend = c(paste("speaker", spk), "", "plug-in Bayes boundary"),
       col = c(class_cols3, NA, "black"), pch = c(16, 16, 16, NA, NA),
       lty = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 2), lwd = 2, seg.len = 2, x.intersp = 0.7,  # Reduces symbol-to-text spacing
       text.width = c(rep(0.12, 3), 0.03, 0.25))                         # Adjust column widths manually

par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (dn in names(drops)) {
  d <- drops[[dn]]
  pred_lda   <- max.col(couple_predict_partial(Xg3, d["i"], d["j"], d["k"], lda_log_odds))
  pred_firth <- max.col(couple_predict_partial(Xg3, d["i"], d["j"], d["k"], firth_log_odds))
  plot_argmax_panel(pred_lda,   paste0("LDA, ", drop_titles[dn]))
  plot_argmax_panel(pred_firth, paste0("Firth Logistic, ", drop_titles[dn]))
}
```

The partial-coupling experiment in @fig-partial-coupling shows that Firth logistic regression is substantially more sensitive to the removal of a pairwise comparison than LDA. We now explain this behaviour through multiplicative miscalibration. When the pair $(i,j)$ is dropped, the third class $k$ becomes a *linkage class*, and the coupled odds can be recovered only as
$$
\frac{p(i)}{p(j)}
=
\frac{p(i)}{p(k)}
\cdot
\frac{p(k)}{p(j)},
$$ {#eq-odds}
so the two remaining classifiers, $i$--$k$ and $j$--$k$, enter only through their estimates of $p(k)$. With LDA as the reference, we compute the multiplicative miscalibration of the linkage class $k$ on the $i$--$k$ classifier on the test points of class $i$ and the $j$--$k$ classifier on those of class $j$, so the $k$ is the less likely class as shown in @fig-miscal-box. If both classifiers were equally miscalibrated, their errors would cancel in @eq-odds and the coupled odds would be unaffected; if the miscalibration is unequal, the remaining imbalance distorts $p(i)/p(j)$ and can cause test points to be misclassified. 


```{r}
#| label: fig-miscal-box
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: Multiplicative miscalibration $\log_{10}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{Firth}}(k)/p_{\mathrm{LDA}}(k)\bigr)$ of the linkage class $k$ when the pair $(i,j)$ is dropped. The dashed red line marks perfect calibration relative to the LDA baseline; the difference between the two medians is shown above each dropped pair.
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

layout(1)   # reset the multi-panel layout left over from fig-partial-coupling
pos <- c(1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8)
top <- max(sapply(link, function(l) max(l$v)))
bot <- min(0, sapply(link, function(l) min(l$v)))
par(mar = c(6.2, 4.8, 1.5, 1))
boxplot(lapply(link, `[[`, "v"), at = pos, xlim = c(0.4, 8.6), ylim = c(bot, top * 1.2),
        names = FALSE, las = 1,
        col = adjustcolor(class_cols3[sapply(link, `[[`, "cls")], alpha.f = 0.55),
        ylab = expression(log[10](p[Firth](k) / p[LDA](k))))
mtext(sapply(link, `[[`, "lab"), side = 1, line = 1.8, at = pos, cex = 0.75)
abline(h = 0, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = c(3, 6), col = "grey80")
for (g in seq_along(link_diff)) {
  x1 <- pos[2 * g - 1]; x2 <- pos[2 * g]; y <- top * 1.08
  segments(x1, y, x2, y); segments(c(x1, x2), y, c(x1, x2), y - top * 0.025)
  text(mean(c(x1, x2)), y, sprintf("difference = %.2f", link_diff[g]), pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
  mtext(link_lab[g], side = 1, line = 4.3, at = mean(c(x1, x2)), cex = 0.8, font = 2)
}
```

For every dropped pair, both Firth classifiers overestimate the linkage class, but not by the same amount. The reason lies in the separation of the classes. As @fig-firth-dscan shows, the multiplicative miscalibration of a Firth classifier grows with the separation of its two classes. The two bridging classifiers, $i$--$k$ and $j$--$k$, are trained on pairs of classes that are separated to different degrees, so they inflate $p(k)$ by different amounts: the larger the difference between their Mahalanobis distances, the larger the imbalance left in @eq-odds. The two extreme cases make this concrete. When $(A,S)$ is dropped, the bridging pairs $A$--$M$ and $S$--$M$ differ most in separation (Mahalanobis distance of $`r f2(d_tr[["A-M"]])`$ against $`r f2(d_tr[["M-S"]])`$); their miscalibrations differ by $`r f2(link_diff[["drop13"]])`$ orders of magnitude, and the Firth coupling loses the most accuracy. When $(M,S)$ is dropped, the bridging pairs $M$--$A$ and $S$--$A$ are almost equally separated ($`r f2(d_tr[["A-M"]])`$ against $`r f2(d_tr[["A-S"]])`$); the imbalance is only $`r f2(link_diff[["drop23"]])`$, and the accuracy is unchanged. Whether an imbalance actually misclassifies points depends, in addition, on the dropped pair itself: the closer the classes $i$ and $j$ are, the smaller the imbalance needed to push points of one into the other. The coupling therefore fails not because one classifier is miscalibrated, but because the two bridging classifiers are miscalibrated unequally.


## Out-of-distribution-detection

Most neural networks for classification are trained using supervised fashion, meaning one provides a set samples $\mathbf{x}_i$ with labels $y_i$. The labels belong to a discrete set, which we can identify with This is a problem when a neural network should detect that its input is something it has never seen before. For instance, an automated driving system should be able detect that something is ahead on the road that it is unable to correctly classify, because it has not seen such object in a training set. A very simple method is to threshold the predicted probability--so-called maximum softmax probability method. Studies has shown that this simple method performs very well in practice [@hendrycks2016baseline, @yang2022openood]. If however, a model provided incorrect predictions by several orders of magnitude, the car would require corrective action (stopping or remote assistance) too frequently.
